paragraphs: This paper develops a framework that learns a prediction model together with a model that explains its behavior. The explanations use high-level attributes intended to be understandable to people. They describe both individual predictions and the predictor more broadly, while aiming to preserve predictive accuracy.

The interpreter builds a small dictionary of attribute functions from the outputs of selected hidden layers. These attributes then feed a linear classifier, creating a relatively direct connection between the learned attributes and the interpretation model's decisions. An entropy-based penalty encourages concise attribute activations, while additional requirements keep the interpretation faithful to the predictor's inputs and outputs.

The authors also develop a visualization pipeline for inspecting the learned features. The framework can train interpretable models jointly or be adapted to explain an already trained network. Evaluations against several leading methods across multiple datasets support its effectiveness in both settings. The contribution is a way to make explanation learning part of the modeling process while also supporting explanations after training.
neurips-2021-a-framework-to-learn-with-i.tldr: A jointly trained interpreter explains neural-network predictions through concise high-level attributes with minimal accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Training a structured neural network can involve penalties that are nonsmooth or nonconvex. These penalties complicate optimization because the training objective need not behave like a smooth loss. This paper studies stochastic proximal gradient methods, which handle regularization through a dedicated optimization step, and asks how to combine them with adaptive gradient updates.

The proposed framework permits arbitrary positive preconditioners and lower semicontinuous regularizers. Preconditioners adjust how updates act in different parameter directions, so their effect must also enter the proximal computation. The authors derive a proximal version of Adam and revise ProxQuant so that its treatment of quantization penalties incorporates these adjustments.

The paper provides convergence guarantees and shows that adaptive methods can improve convergence constants over ordinary SGD for sparse data. Experiments favor stochastic proximal methods over subgradient approaches, with the advantage appearing larger for nonconvex penalties than for convex ones. Together, these results support treating adaptivity and regularization as coupled parts of the update rather than designing their effects independently.
neurips-2021-adaptive-proximal-gradient-.tldr: A stochastic proximal optimization framework combines adaptive updates with nonsmooth regularization and yields proximal Adam and an improved ProxQuant.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions in which rewards have a linear structure but the constraints can be nonlinear. The learner seeks high cumulative expected reward while satisfying constraints at each round. The challenge is to learn which actions are rewarding while also managing the restrictions imposed on those actions.

The proposed algorithm uses a primal-dual optimization approach. Its primal component follows LinUCB, a method for stochastic linear bandits, while its dual component handles the constraints. The extra computational work depends on the number of constraints but is independent of the sizes of the context, action, and feature spaces. Overall computation therefore remains similar to that of unconstrained LinUCB.

The analysis gives a pseudo-regret bound growing roughly with the square root of elapsed rounds, with dependence on feature dimension, constraint count, and a Slater constant. It also establishes zero constraint violation after a threshold round that does not depend on the total horizon. This is an eventual guarantee: the abstract does not claim zero violations from the first round.
neurips-2021-an-efficient-pessimistic-op.tldr: A primal-dual linear-bandit algorithm combines efficient reward learning with zero constraint violations after a horizon-independent threshold.

paragraphs: The optimization procedure used to train a model can affect how well that model performs beyond its training data. This paper analyzes that connection for stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, or SGLD. It derives a generalization bound by relating the algorithm to Gaussian communication channels from information theory.

The resulting bound can be calculated using training data and includes gradient variance. That variance measures a particular form of sharpness in the loss landscape, connecting the behavior of training gradients to a guarantee about generalization. Numerical experiments show that the bound can predict the behavior of the actual gap between training and generalization performance.

The authors also analyze differentially private SGD. When only the final iterate is released and intermediate iterates remain hidden, they strengthen the bound with a factor that decays over time. Strong data processing inequalities establish this effect, which reduces the contribution of earlier training iterations to the bound. The result concerns this specific output setting and gives a mathematical account of how iteration can improve the generalization guarantee.
neurips-2021-analyzing-the-generalizatio.tldr: Gaussian-channel analysis yields data-computable generalization bounds for SGLD and tighter final-iterate bounds for DP-SGD.

paragraphs: Benign overfitting describes situations where a model fits its training data exactly yet still generalizes well. This paper studies that possibility in multiclass linear classification, extending attention beyond regression and binary classification. It considers separable data and compares three common ways of training classifiers.

The methods are cross-entropy training, which converges to a multiclass support vector machine solution; least-squares training, which converges to a minimum-norm interpolating solution; and one-vs-all support vector machines. Under a sufficient condition, all three produce classifiers that interpolate the training data and have equal accuracy. For Gaussian-mixture and multinomial-logistic data models, sufficiently high effective overparameterization makes that condition hold.

The authors then derive accuracy bounds for the minimum-norm interpolating classifier. Combined with the equivalence result, these bounds establish benign overfitting for all three methods under sufficient overparameterization. The findings show that support vector machine solutions can generalize well in regimes beyond those explained by typical margin-based bounds. They do not assert that interpolation guarantees good generalization for arbitrary data.
neurips-2021-benign-overfitting-in-multi.tldr: Under sufficient overparameterization and stated data conditions, three multiclass linear classifiers interpolate training data while generalizing well.

paragraphs: Cross-validation is widely used to choose the regularization strength in ridge regression. Even if the best cross-validation setting corresponds to good performance on new data, finding that setting is a separate optimization problem. This paper investigates the shape of the cross-validation loss and whether it supports reliable global optimization.

The authors show that the loss need not be quasiconvex and may contain multiple local optima. Consequently, the familiar simplicity of ridge regression does not automatically carry over to tuning its regularization parameter. They also identify a sufficient favorable case: quasiconvexity is guaranteed when the covariate matrix has a nearly flat spectrum and response noise is not too high.

The analysis separates data properties that affect quasiconvexity from those that do not. Response norm, right singular vectors of the covariate matrix, and overall singular-value scaling do not determine its status, while the remaining dependencies are more complex. Simulations confirm the theoretical findings. The contribution clarifies when the tuning objective has a useful shape and why that shape cannot be presumed universally.
neurips-2021-can-we-globally-optimize-cr.tldr: Ridge cross-validation loss can have multiple local optima, though nearly flat covariate spectra and sufficiently low noise guarantee quasiconvexity.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic gradient descent can reduce gradient variance by combining updates from multiple workers, but frequent communication can consume the resulting speed gains. This paper assumes that all workers share the same dataset and coordinate through a central server. It studies how rarely they can communicate while retaining favorable convergence.

The proposed Local SGD schedule makes communication less frequent as training progresses. The analysis achieves error scaling as 1/(NT), where N is the number of workers and T is the number of local steps, with a communication count independent of T. A count scaling with N is sufficient. Simulations in which the count scales as the square root or three-quarter power of N fail to achieve linear speedup, suggesting that the analyzed requirement is close to tight.

The paper also examines averaging only once, at the end. Under mild assumptions, especially twice differentiability near the optimal solution, this one-shot method attains the optimal convergence rate asymptotically. That final result is conditional and asymptotic, distinct from the communication guarantee for the proposed Local SGD schedule.
neurips-2021-communication-efficient-sgd.tldr: Decreasing communication frequency preserves favorable Local SGD convergence, while one-shot averaging is asymptotically optimal under additional assumptions.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network involves deciding which variables depend on which others. A Bayesian approach also represents uncertainty about those connections, rather than committing to a single graph. This paper introduces DiBS, a differentiable framework for learning such distributions over network structures from data.

DiBS works in a continuous latent space that represents a probabilistic graph. This makes differentiable inference possible while retaining uncertainty over structure. The framework does not require one particular form for each variable's conditional distribution. It can jointly infer the graph and the parameters governing those distributions, including nonlinear dependencies represented by neural networks.

Using this formulation, the authors develop a general-purpose variational inference method to approximate distributions over structural models. Evaluations on simulated and real-world data show substantial improvements over related joint posterior inference approaches. The method matters because uncertainty about connections and uncertainty about their parameters can be handled together. Such structural uncertainty is relevant to active causal discovery and intervention design, which motivate the work.
neurips-2021-dibs-differentiable-bayesia.tldr: DiBS uses a continuous probabilistic graph representation to jointly infer Bayesian network structures and parameters through differentiable inference.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a neural network can be approximated by querying it as a black box. The learner can choose inputs and observe the network's outputs, a stronger form of access than receiving random labeled examples. Model extraction provides one motivation for studying this setting.

The target can be any neural network with one hidden layer and ReLU activations. The authors give an algorithm that produces another network with low squared error relative to the target, measured under a Gaussian input distribution. Both the number of queries and the running time are polynomial in all problem parameters, giving a formal efficiency guarantee.

The result establishes a provable basis for a task that earlier security research had explored empirically. Its guarantee concerns approximation of the target's outputs under the stated measure, rather than exact recovery of its internal parameters. The architectural and distributional scope is central: the abstract supports a result for one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with Gaussian-measured error, not a general extraction theorem for every neural architecture.
neurips-2021-efficiently-learning-one-hi.tldr: A polynomial-time query algorithm approximates any one-hidden-layer ReLU network with low squared error under a Gaussian input measure.

paragraphs: Low-rank tensor decompositions represent multidimensional data in a more compact form, but computing them can be expensive. Alternating least squares repeatedly solves large least-squares problems, making it costly for large, sparse tensors. This paper develops a randomized version for Tucker decomposition that replaces those subproblems with smaller sketches.

The sketched subproblems include a rank constraint. For TensorSketch and leverage-score sampling, the authors provide upper bounds on sketch sizes sufficient to obtain relative subproblem error proportional to a chosen accuracy parameter. They also introduce an initialization method based on a randomized range finder. Together, these components achieve decomposition accuracy comparable to standard higher-order orthogonal iteration in experiments.

Across synthetic and real datasets, the method improves the relative decomposition residual by up to 22.0% over a leading sketched Tucker algorithm. The authors also use randomized Tucker compression before performing CP decomposition on the smaller core tensor. Experiments show faster convergence and more accurate CP decompositions. The theoretical guarantees concern individual sketched subproblems, while the overall decomposition improvements are empirical findings.
neurips-2021-fast-and-accurate-randomize.tldr: Randomized sketching and initialization accelerate Tucker decomposition and also improve CP decomposition through Tucker compression.

paragraphs: Incorrect class labels can undermine neural-network training. One response is to identify unreliable examples and change how they are used, but many detectors rely on heuristic judgments based on prediction losses. This paper proposes FINE, a detector that instead examines the learned representations of training examples.

FINE measures how each representation aligns with the latent representation distribution. It obtains the relevant directions through an eigendecomposition of the data Gram matrix, using relationships among representations to identify potentially noisy instances. The authors describe the resulting detector as simple and derivative-free, and provide theoretical guarantees for their framework.

The paper applies FINE in three ways: selecting training samples, supporting a semi-supervised learning approach, and combining it with noise-robust loss functions. Experiments across benchmark datasets show improvements over the corresponding baselines in all three applications. These findings support representation alignment as a useful signal for detecting label noise and show that the detector can complement several different strategies for learning from imperfect labels.
neurips-2021-fine-samples-for-learning-w.tldr: FINE detects noisy labels through eigenvector-based representation alignment and improves three approaches to learning with label noise.

paragraphs: Finding a good input to a black-box function is different from certifying how close that input is to optimal. This paper studies both requirements together for Lipschitz functions on compact subsets of a finite-dimensional space. Algorithms observe function values and must return an approximate maximizer with an accuracy certificate.

Under a weak assumption on the domain, the authors characterize the required number of evaluations through an integral involving the gap between each function value and the maximum, the target accuracy, and the dimension. This makes the bound depend on the particular function being optimized. Regions close to the maximum contribute differently from regions whose values are clearly worse.

The upper bound connects packing arguments for the Piyavskii-Shubert algorithm to this integral. A certified version of the computationally tractable DOO algorithm matches the packing and integral bounds. A complementary instance-dependent lower bound uses local worst-case analysis. Together, these results characterize the cost of finding and certifying a solution, extending a previously partial one-dimensional understanding to the stated higher-dimensional setting.
neurips-2021-instance-dependent-bounds-f.tldr: Instance-dependent bounds characterize the function evaluations needed to find and certify an approximate maximum of a Lipschitz function.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian method for learning nonlinear operators: mappings that transform input functions into output functions. Its nonparametric Volterra kernels model, or NVKM, uses a Volterra series and represents the series' kernels with Gaussian processes. This provides a flexible probabilistic representation of the operator.

The model supports two settings. When the input function is hidden and given a Gaussian-process prior, it can perform regression with one or several outputs and acts as a nonlinear, nonparametric latent force model. When the input is observed, it can instead identify the system that maps those inputs to outputs.

The computational method samples explicit functions from Gaussian processes and passes these realizations through the Volterra series without numerical integration. Doubly stochastic variational inference supports scalability, and the method avoids requiring Gaussian approximations for the output processes. Evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate applications to multiple-output regression and system identification. The contribution combines uncertainty-aware nonlinear operator learning with an inference strategy that addresses the computation needed to use it.
neurips-2021-learning-nonparametric-volt.tldr: NVKM combines Gaussian-process Volterra kernels with efficient sampling to learn nonlinear operators for regression and system identification.

paragraphs: Exact mixed-integer programming solvers can eventually find optimal solutions, but practical decisions often require good solutions much earlier. Primal heuristics help supply those solutions during search. This paper focuses on how a solver schedules its available heuristics, rather than on designing another individual heuristic.

Solvers commonly manage heuristics through fixed rules developed from broad empirical testing. Because a heuristic's usefulness depends on the problem, those general rules may be a poor fit for a particular problem class. The authors instead learn a problem-specific schedule from data describing heuristic performance, seeking a collection of heuristic executions that finds many solutions at low cost.

The paper formalizes this scheduling task and provides an efficient algorithm for computing a schedule. Against the default configuration of a leading academic solver, the learned schedules reduce average primal integral by up to 49% on two challenging instance classes. This supports using performance data to improve the timing and coordination of existing heuristics. The reported reduction concerns the evaluated classes and metric, rather than a universal solver speedup.
neurips-2021-learning-to-schedule-heuris.tldr: Learning problem-specific heuristic schedules improves early solution finding in an exact mixed-integer programming solver.

paragraphs: Few-shot meta-learners can adapt to new tasks with little test-time computation, yet training them can require substantial memory. An entire task's support set must be processed before an optimization step, making large tasks with large images difficult to accommodate. This paper introduces LITE, an episodic training scheme designed to make such training possible on one GPU.

LITE uses a decomposition of the task gradient into contributions from its training images. It performs a forward pass over the complete training set but backpropagates through only a randomly selected subset. The authors show that this produces an unbiased approximation of the full gradient while substantially reducing memory use.

Meta-learners trained with LITE achieve new leading accuracy on ORBIT and three of four parts of VTAB+MD relative to leading meta-learners. They also become competitive with transfer-learning approaches while using a fraction of the test-time computation. These findings show how reducing training memory requirements can make the benefits of large-image meta-learning accessible without sacrificing its computationally economical adaptation.
neurips-2021-memory-efficient-meta-learn.tldr: LITE reduces meta-training memory through unbiased subset backpropagation, enabling large-image tasks on a single GPU.

paragraphs: MLP-Mixer asks whether strong image classification requires either convolutions or attention. The paper presents an architecture built entirely from multilayer perceptrons, showing that these familiar vision mechanisms are not necessary for competitive performance in the evaluated training settings. Its contribution is a different architectural route to combining visual information.

The model uses two types of layers. One applies multilayer perceptrons independently within image patches, mixing features at each location. The other operates across patches, mixing information between spatial locations. Separating these two operations lets the network combine local feature information and information distributed across the image using the same basic family of building blocks.

With large training datasets or modern regularization schemes, MLP-Mixer achieves competitive image-classification results. Its pretraining and inference costs are comparable to those of leading models. These conditions matter: the claim is about performance with the stated training support, not superiority in every setting. The findings broaden the set of architectures worth investigating beyond the established convolutional and attention-based approaches.
neurips-2021-mlp-mixer-an-all-mlp-archit.tldr: MLP-Mixer achieves competitive image classification using only multilayer perceptrons that mix within-patch features and information across patches.

paragraphs: This paper learns mappings from the inputs of partial differential equations to their solutions. Instead of treating each solution as an unrelated prediction, it models the inverse operator between function spaces. The proposed neural operator uses multiwavelets to compress and represent the operator's kernel efficiently.

The method embeds inverse multiwavelet filters and learns the kernel's projection onto fixed polynomial bases. Repeated multiwavelet transforms create several scales at which the projected kernel is trained. This allows the model to capture dependencies at different scales and produces a resolution-independent scheme. Learning a function-space mapping also allows it to process higher-resolution inputs after training on lower-resolution data.

Experiments cover Korteweg-de Vries, Burgers', Darcy flow, and Navier-Stokes equations. The authors report higher accuracy than existing neural operator approaches and leading results across a range of datasets. For time-varying equations, they report improvements of two to ten times, including relative L2 errors of 0.0018 for Burgers' and 0.0033 for Korteweg-de Vries. These results support the value of explicitly building multiscale kernel structure into operator learning.
neurips-2021-multiwavelet-based-operator.tldr: A multiwavelet neural operator learns differential-equation solution maps across scales and supports higher-resolution prediction from lower-resolution training.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model patterns whose points tend to repel one another. They are useful partly because sampling and inference remain tractable, an unusual combination for models of negative dependence. This paper addresses learning such processes when points occupy a continuous domain and the model is not restricted to a fixed parametric family.

The main obstacle is that nonparametric maximum likelihood involves optimization over trace-class operators, an infinite-dimensional problem. The authors show that a restricted version fits a representer theorem for nonnegative functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This produces a finite-dimensional optimization problem with strong statistical connections to the original maximum-likelihood formulation.

The paper proposes, analyzes, and demonstrates a fixed-point algorithm for that finite problem. It also provides a controlled estimate of the process's correlation kernel, making the fitted model more interpretable. The contribution therefore links a continuous statistical estimation problem to a concrete computational procedure. Its reduction applies to the stated restricted formulation, rather than claiming an unrestricted solution to every continuous DPP likelihood problem.
neurips-2021-nonparametric-estimation-of.tldr: A representer theorem reduces restricted nonparametric continuous-DPP estimation to a finite problem with a fixed-point solver.

paragraphs: This paper asks which learning problems can, in principle, be solved by minibatch SGD applied to differentiable models or neural networks. It compares that paradigm with statistical-query learning and with general sample-based learning in the PAC framework. The analysis identifies gradient precision and minibatch size as decisive factors.

SGD can always simulate statistical-query learning. When the product of batch size b and the gradient precision parameter rho is sufficiently small, it can also simulate any sample-based learning algorithm, matching PAC learning power. This extends an earlier result for single-example batches. If rho is exponentially small, corresponding to polynomially many precision bits, the simulation works regardless of batch size.

In another regime, where b times rho squared is sufficiently large, SGD has exactly statistical-query learning power. Thus, the abstract gives different equivalence results under different precision and batch-size conditions. These are statements about what the learning paradigm can represent through simulation, rather than a claim that an ordinary training setup automatically finds every learnable solution.
neurips-2021-on-the-power-of-differentia.tldr: SGD's theoretical learning power ranges from statistical-query learning to full PAC learning depending on gradient precision and minibatch size.

paragraphs: Deep Markov models use neural networks to make Markov-style generative modeling more expressive. Their flexibility raises a basic question about dynamics: under what conditions is their stochastic behavior stable? This paper develops a stability analysis and gives sufficient conditions that guarantee stability for the models considered.

The analysis examines contraction in probabilistic maps represented by deep networks. It connects the spectral properties of network weight matrices and the choice of activation functions to stability and overall dynamics. The stated treatment concerns deep Markov models with Gaussian distributions, making the probabilistic setting part of the scope of the results.

Building on the theory, the authors propose practical ways to constrain model design so that stability is guaranteed. Numerical experiments using those constraints support the theoretical conclusions. The value of the work is the link between mathematical properties of neural-network components and controlled behavior of the resulting stochastic model. Because the conditions are sufficient, the results provide routes to stable designs without claiming that every stable model must satisfy those same constraints.
neurips-2021-on-the-stochastic-stability.tldr: Contraction-based analysis gives sufficient stability conditions and practical design constraints for Gaussian deep Markov models.

paragraphs: Implicit models can represent computations corresponding to infinitely many layers. Training them has commonly involved implicit differentiation to compute an exact gradient for backpropagation, which can be expensive. This paper asks whether a cheaper gradient estimate can serve as an effective training signal.

The proposed phantom gradient avoids the costly exact-gradient computation. The authors analyze conditions under which an ascent direction in the loss landscape can be found and give two implementations, based on damped unrolling and a Neumann series. These provide concrete ways to construct lightweight gradient estimates for implicit-model training.

Experiments on large-scale tasks show backward-pass acceleration of roughly 1.7 times. On ImageNet, the method also improves performance over approaches using the exact gradient. The empirical result is therefore about both reduced backward computation and the usefulness of the resulting update direction. The paper does not establish that every approximate gradient is preferable; it supplies particular constructions, theoretical conditions, and experimental evidence for the phantom-gradient approach.
neurips-2021-on-training-implicit-models.tldr: Phantom gradients replace expensive exact gradients in implicit models, accelerating backward passes and improving ImageNet performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Deep hashing learns binary codes for retrieval. Training usually needs to make those codes discriminative while keeping the continuous representations close to their binary versions. Additional requirements can introduce several more losses, creating a difficult balancing problem. This paper proposes a hashing model trained with a single objective.

The objective maximizes cosine similarity between continuous codes and corresponding binary orthogonal codes. The authors show that this can provide both discriminative codes and quantization-error minimization. Within the same design, a batch-normalization layer supplies code balancing, while label smoothing makes multilabel classification straightforward. These components avoid the need to tune relative weights for multiple losses.

Experiments on three large-scale instance-retrieval benchmarks show that the model outperforms leading multiloss hashing approaches, often by substantial margins. The result supports simplifying the training objective without giving up the competing properties required of useful hash codes. Its significance lies in using the structure of the target binary codes to make one similarity objective serve several learning requirements.
neurips-2021-one-loss-for-all-deep-hashi.tldr: A single cosine-similarity objective learns discriminative binary hash codes while minimizing quantization error and simplifying training.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes and their relationships into vectors for analysis and machine learning. Many methods learn from context nodes sampled through random walks. This paper examines how the graph's structure biases that sampling process and, in turn, influences the representations that are learned.

A prominent example is degree bias: random walks sample nodes in proportion to their degree. As a result, the contexts used for embedding reflect this structural sampling preference. The authors propose residual2vec, a general embedding method that uses random graphs to account for various structural biases. The choice to model those biases explicitly is central to the approach.

The reported demonstrations show improved link prediction and clustering after debiasing. They also show that the method enables explicit modeling of salient structural graph properties in the embedding. This makes the contribution broader than a correction for node degree alone. It provides a way to account for structural effects in context sampling while retaining graph representations useful for the downstream tasks examined.
neurips-2021-residual2vec-debiasing-grap.tldr: Residual2vec uses random graphs to account for structural sampling biases and improves graph link prediction and clustering.

paragraphs: Typical neural-network training updates every parameter at every iteration. Updating only a small subset can reduce the storage and communication associated with those updates. This paper studies how to choose a sparse subset that can remain fixed over many training iterations, rather than requiring continual changes to the selection.

The method selects the k parameters with the largest Fisher information and uses them to construct a binary update mask. Fisher information serves as a simple approximation of which parameters matter most for the task. The mask determines which parameters receive updates, making the contribution a method for sparse training updates rather than a claim about removing the remaining model parameters.

Experiments cover parameter-efficient transfer learning and distributed training. The approach matches or exceeds other sparse-update methods while reducing memory usage and communication costs. These findings suggest that a task-informed, fixed selection can retain useful training capacity with fewer resources devoted to updates. The abstract reports these advantages in the evaluated settings without claiming that the same subset is best for every task.
neurips-2021-training-neural-networks-wi.tldr: Fixed masks based on Fisher information select a small parameter subset for efficient training with competitive sparse-update performance.

paragraphs: VATT learns representations from unlabeled video, audio, and text using Transformers without convolutions. It takes raw signals and trains end to end from scratch with multimodal contrastive losses. The aim is to learn representations that transfer to several tasks without supervised pretraining.

The evaluation includes video action recognition, audio event classification, image classification, and text-to-video retrieval. The authors also investigate sharing one Transformer's weights across all three modalities. This explores whether a common backbone can process these different input types within the same overall framework.

The reported results outperform leading convolution-based architectures on downstream tasks. Video recognition reaches 82.1%, 83.6%, and 72.7% top-1 accuracy on the three Kinetics benchmarks, and 41.1% on Moments in Time. Transfer to ImageNet achieves 78.7%, compared with 64.7% when the same Transformer is trained there from scratch. The audio model reaches 39.4% mean average precision on AudioSet. These results support the usefulness of multimodal self-supervised representations, including transfer from video training to image classification.
neurips-2021-vatt-transformers-for-multi.tldr: VATT learns transferable video, audio, and text representations from unlabeled raw inputs using convolution-free Transformers.
